extracted.intended_audience: general public, journalists, policymakers, and mine-safety professionals
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic article documenting a specific coal mine explosion (the Sago Mine disaster), its background, timeline, investigation, regulatory responses, and media coverage. Serves as a reference summary for readers seeking facts and context about the incident and ensuing safety/regulatory issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seal construction standard (MSHA requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: MSHA rules seals to be built using "solid concrete blocks" or alternate materials that will withstand 20 pounds per square inch of pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article contrasts this requirement with state approval of dense foam "Omega blocks" that could reportedly withhold pressures of five pounds per square inch. NIOSH research is cited showing that 4 ft thick pumped cement seals approved by MSHA effectively contained an explosion in another mine. After Sago, MSHA tested alternative seals and imposed a temporary moratorium on all alternative seal construction pending testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-contained self-rescuer (SCSR) requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Miners are required to carry an SCSR that provides a one-hour supply of oxygen for evacuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes variation in functionality (at least four emergency oxygen packs were not functioning at Sago). Emergency supplies were stored in 55-gallon drums in the mine. The SCSR one-hour supply is the regulatory expectation for miner evacuation capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significant/Serious and Substantial (S&S) violation classification
rubrics_metrics.description: S&S violations are those that MSHA believes are likely to cause an accident that would seriously injure a miner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites MSHA statistics (e.g., Sago had 208 citations in 2005, 96 considered S&S) and the Charleston Gazette explanation of S&S. High counts of S&S violations are presented as indicators of potentially serious safety problems rather than mere paperwork errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with approved roof control, ventilation and escapeway plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Violations included failure to follow the approved roof control and mine ventilation plans and problems concerning emergency escapeways and required pre-shift safety examinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These particular program elements (roof control, ventilation, escapeways, pre-shift exams) are cited as specific regulatory and operational areas where noncompliance can lead to citations and increased risk of accidents; MSHA enforcement actions targeted these deficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: MSHA investigation procedures and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: MSHA's investigative team will examine the site, interview mine personnel and others with information, review records and plans, inspect any equipment involved and issue any citations for violations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes MSHA launching an independent eight-member technical team, public hearings, joint federal-state investigations, and potential issuance of citations. It also notes that MSHA intends to publish transcripts and make full investigative reports available to families and the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rescue operation safety procedures and pacing
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of hazardous atmospheres (CO, methane) rescuers waited until gas levels abated; progress was limited to about 1,000 feet (300 m) per hour, with checks every 500 feet (150 m), and communications protocols (disconnecting telephones between checkpoints) to avoid sparking another explosion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains that high CO and methane forced caution (12-hour wait), use of boreholes to test air and lower cameras/microphones, and that some mechanical actions (hot drill bits, powered equipment) could ignite methane. A 1,300 lb robot was deployed but retrieved when mired. These operational choices are presented as safety-driven constraints on rescue speed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmospheric hazard thresholds for rescue decisions (CO levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Air quality tests showed 1,300 parts per million (ppm) of carbon monoxide near the miners (more than 200 ppm is considered unsafe). CO levels of 300–400 ppm were near the safe threshold to support life for about 15 minutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These numeric thresholds are used in the article to illustrate why rescuers delayed entry and assess survivability; they function as operational criteria for rescue timing and tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirement: barricading and signaling in entrapment scenarios
rubrics_metrics.description: Miners are trained to find a safe part of the mine and barricade themselves into it in the event of an explosion or collapse, and to use SCSRs and signal to the surface (for example by hammering on bolts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sole survivor's account describes erecting a curtain, attempting to signal by pounding on bolts, sharing rescuers, writing letters, and praying—illustrating expected behaviors and how they can be constrained by conditions (bad air, nonfunctional rescuers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation factors and investigative hypotheses to be evaluated
rubrics_metrics.description: Potential causes to be investigated include lightning strike near the mine entrance igniting methane, seismic activity correlating with lightning, proximity of active gas and oil wells to sealed areas, use of foam rather than concrete seals, and sparks from restarting machinery after a holiday.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists these early theories and the evidence considered (lightning detection network data, seismic sensors, permit records showing gas wells, reports about Omega blocks), indicating the types of technical and factual criteria investigators will weigh when determining cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: FOIA policy on release of MSHA inspector notes
rubrics_metrics.description: MSHA had changed a prior policy of routinely releasing inspector notes under FOIA; after criticism, Acting Assistant Secretary David G. Dye concluded that inspector notes should generally be released once a citation has been issued (or an inspection is closed without citations), rather than withholding the notes until all litigation is concluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article presents this as a transparency and accountability standard affecting public access to inspection records and the ability of journalists, operators, and miners to understand past violations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory response: Emergency Mine Evacuation rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: Following the Sago disaster MSHA pursued new mine evacuation rules via special rulemaking action and issued an "Emergency Mine Evacuation; Final Rule" (30 CFR Parts 48, 50, and 75).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article references Federal Register notices and press releases about emergency evacuation rulemaking as an example of regulatory standards and procedural changes triggered by the incident.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational indicators of elevated risk (inspection/enforcement intensity and accident rates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicators of elevated risk at Sago included mining operations doubling between 2004 and 2005, an injury rate significantly above the national average (Sago accident rate 17.04 in 2005 vs national average 5.66), and a sharp increase (84%) in on-site inspection presence and enforcement actions by MSHA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article uses these quantitative operational and enforcement metrics to argue that high violation and accident rates should 'tip off' management and regulators that systemic safety problems exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and approval of investigation participants (union participation rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory/administrative rules and court orders governing participation by parties in investigations — illustrated by ICG objecting to UMWA participation and a federal judge ordering ICG to allow UMWA officials to enter the mine because "the public interest is best served by a complete and thorough investigation".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This entry captures procedural standards about who may participate in investigations, the legal basis for allowing miner/union involvement, and the balancing of company objections against public interest in thorough investigations.
